items.title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.original_title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.rss_title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.rss_description: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy PaulCarroll Mon, 11/02/2026 - 11:30 Bill Gates recently said he is using generative AI as part of the annual, two-week strategy session that determines how the Gates Foundation spends its next $10 billion. He'll be "taking the strategy notes and actually engaging in a dialogue with ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, and even having them talk with each other," he said. I don't have $10 billion that I'm considering how to spend, and you may not, either, but genAI has now improved to the point where it can at least be an aid in setting strategy at almost any level. An old boss, Mel Bergstein, used to say: "Strategy is what you don't do." The idea worked for Mel, who founded a consulting firm, Diamond Management & Technology Partners, that pioneered the notion of digital strategy in the mid-1990s. Chunka Mui and I took Mel's adage further in our book, "Billion Dollar Lessons," for which we had 20 researchers spend two years looking at 2,500 major failures to identify the warning signs. Our recommended solution boiled down to having a "devil's advocate" identify all the underlying assumptions for a strategy, to keep problems from being glossed over as an executive team rushed to realize the CEO's plan. GenAI, used right, can now do a pretty good job of filling that role for anyone. Let's have a look. Gates told the New York Times that, "i n a few of the reviews, we’ll actually have the A.I. sit in. In a few cases, we’ll tell it: Hey, only speak if we ask you. And then in a few other cases, we’ll say: Hey, if you hear something you think is wrong or you hear us thinking about, for example, what are these statistics? Please engage. So we’ve gone from it being a joke [when someone suggested using genAI a year ago] to it will be a peer — not making any final decisions, but it will be a peer in deep, complex strategic discussions, making a significant contribution." I'm not willing to go that far just yet, partly because I'd need to test the domain knowledge that the large language models have about a subtle, heavily regulated business like insurance and partly because genAI has shown itself to be a sycophant. The biggest, overarching pattern of failure that Chunka and I found in the research for " Billion Dollar Lessons " was that people were reluctant to point out obvious problems that could derail initiatives that had the imprimatur of the CEO, and we don't want to replace human sycophants with AI ones. But you can describe your strategy to an AI, then pepper it with questions, going deeper each time while demanding evidence for its thinking and insisting it be blunt. Let's say you're thinking of buying a company. You could start with a general question: What could go wrong? Then you probe. How will our competitors react? What if interest rates increase? The economy goes into recession? The war in Iran escalates? Will we actually be able to cross-sell to our customers? Will the efficiencies from scale be as great as we expect? Who's done something similar and had problems? What were the problems? And on and on and on. You can do the same exercise if you're thinking of a new line of business, a software overhaul, adopting AI chatbots — or if you want to explore the dangers of standing pat, of not undertaking a major initiative that is under consideration. Major corporations have staff do extensive analysis along the lines I'm suggesting and, in the case of a possible acquisition, draw on their investment banks for advice — but the bias is always toward acting. If the perception is that the CEO backs an idea, the staff strives to make it work, not to kill it. Investment banks only collect their hefty fees if the deal happens, so why would they recommend against it? When Chunka and I did a consulting project with a major company that was considering launching autonomous vehicles, we saw elaborate studies it had commissioned from consulting firms that said the robotaxi business was a slam dunk and that the first to enter would win big. That was more than eight years ago. It turned out, however, that the executives working on the AV project internally were aware of all the sorts of operational and safety issues that we've all seen play out and that have slowed the robotaxi rollout. Those concerns were brought to the surface in the interviews for our devil's advocate review. Warren Buffett used to set aside two, equal pots of money when asking investment banks for advice on possible acquisitions — one for a bank that argued in favor of a deal and one for a bank that argued against it. Whichever carried the day collected its fees, while the other got nothing. You can be sure the "anti" bank worked as hard as possible on its arguments and evidence. In my experience, many big ideas should fall apart at the slightest scrutiny. As we wrote in "Billion Dollar Lessons," we thought 47% of the failures we investigated were based on strategies that never should have made it out of the strategy room — and not because those involved were stupid or inexperienced. The fifth-biggest cement maker in the world reasoned that it was really in the home products business because so much of its cement was used there. It began also making furnaces and lawn mowers... then went bankrupt and was bought by a competitor. Avon decided that its core competency was its culture of caring — not, you know, its line of cosmetics and its devoted salesforce — so it bought a maker of medical equipment and an operator of retirement homes. It had no idea how to operate the new businesses and quickly sold them at a major loss. In the early days of fax machines, FedEx spent hundreds of millions of dollars to set up a business that would collect a document from you, drive it to the nearest office, fax it to the office nearest your destination, then drive the fax to the recipient. The company somehow missed that Moore's law would soon make the devices so inexpensive that every company would have its own. It may take time to learn how to use genAI to avoid costly strategic mistakes — and that's even before we start using it as broadly as Gates is planning to. You'll likely also need to introduce to the LLM information specific to your market, including regulatory issues that it likely doesn't have even as these models try to Hoover up everything available on the internet. Insurance is a complicated market. But I think we're now at the point where genAI can, if managed correctly, start to catch strategic errors. We won't get that 47% figure for obviously bad ideas down to zero, but even heading toward 40%, maybe even 33%, would mark real progress. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll At any level of setting strategy, from the boardroom to the one-person agency, generative AI can bring assumptions to the surface, helping you see what NOT to do. items.rss_title: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating
items.rss_description: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims get the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? Read More Agentic AI Redefines Real-Time Underwriting by Rachita Nahata Real-time underwriting isn't about instant decisions but leveraging agentic AI and current data to help underwriters assess risk faster. Read More Breaking Down Silos in Insurance by Rory Meleniclis Insurers can dismantle organizational silos by shifting from project-based work to product teams built around shared capabilities like underwriting and claims. Read More How AI Can Transform Submissions for Underwriting by Prathap Gokul Commercial insurers face a strategic challenge: identifying which submissions merit scarce underwriting attention, not just processing more faster. Read More Making AI Work in Commercial Submission Intake by Vital Soupel Insurers need a practical blueprint for where to apply AI first, how to move beyond pilots, and how to scale the technology responsibly. Read More Turning Volatility Into Value by Insurance Thought Leadership Amid today's heightened uncertainty, Dawn Miller, chief commercial officer at Lloyd's, explores how insurers can innovate their way to value both for themselves and for their clients. items.summary: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims get the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? items.title: Insurance Fraud Targets Seniors Online
items.original_title: Insurance Fraud Targets Seniors Online
items.rss_title: Insurance Fraud Targets Seniors Online
items.rss_description: Insurance Fraud Targets Seniors Online Life & Health ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 13:16 Scammers increasingly impersonate insurers to steal identities and money during open enrollment. November 12, 2026 Image Last year, the Justice Department brought the largest healthcare fraud case in its history, which included charges that criminals stole the identities of more than 1 million Americans to submit $10.6 billion in fraudulent Medicare claims for urinary catheters. While Medicare blocked nearly all of it, private Medicare supplemental insurers paid out about $900 million. Americans lost a record $20.9 billion to internet crime in 2025, up 26% in one year, according to the FBI. Insurance fraud, including healthcare fraud, costs Americans more than $300 billion a year, and health insurance scams pick up during open enrollment, the FTC says. Seniors are the hardest-hit age group, losing $7.7 billion in 2025, up 59% in one year. In fact, Michigan officials warned on Oct. 12 of impostors claiming to be from Medicare to dupe older adults. As co-founder of Spokeo , a people search company, and former co-chair of the W3C Credentials Community Group , I have witnessed firsthand how scammers have grown increasingly sophisticated over the last 20 years. Insurance scams are evolving and costly We are seeing many insurance-related scams in 2026. Fraudsters are buying sponsored search ads with web addresses and logos that look very similar to HealthCare.gov and Medicare.gov . When Americans click on the link, they end up buying a plan that is not real insurance and also fork over their personal information, which can lead to identity theft. Even large health insurers are being duped, as the $900 million loss in the catheter case shows. The Coalition Against Insurance Fraud calls insurance fraud "the crime we all pay for," because it comes back to honest policyholders as higher premiums, which can hurt retention. In a September survey by BrandShield , 30% of U.S. adults said they would stop buying online from brands scammers had impersonated. For an insurer, that is a renewal lost to a scam it never ran. Here are three tips for insurers to help prevent insurance fraud Say what you will never do. Tell customers you will never ask for a one-time code or take payment by gift card, wire or crypto. Put the statement on the ID card, in the app, and on every renewal notice. Explain what numbers to trust and verify. Scammers can spoof caller ID so your company's name appears on a customer's phone. In every fraud alert, encourage customers to use the number on their card and check the identity of incoming callers with a reverse phone search . Report fake ads and websites and warn consumers. Search regularly for impostors using your name and report them to the FBI IC3 , the FTC , and the online platform where they live. Send alerts to customers in real time. Harrison Tang

items.title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.original_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_description: Why Can't We Fund Prevention? Predict & Prevent ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 09:29 Industrial organizations excel at financing recovery from asset failures but struggle to justify prevention spending with the same economic rigor. November 5, 2026 Image We've built an extraordinarily sophisticated financial system around industrial failure. We can price it, insure it, reserve capital for it, and finance recovery when it happens, but preventing that same failure often requires an entirely different standard of proof. Insurance is exceptionally good at mobilizing money after something goes wrong. Natural catastrophes caused an estimated $100 billion in economic losses in the first half of 2026. Insurance covered approximately 42%, leaving nearly $60 billion to be absorbed elsewhere. Insurance's ability to fund recovery is indispensable. The shortfall also exposes a contradiction in how risk is funded. Premiums, deductibles, and recovery costs have established places in corporate budgets. A proposal to prevent an asset failure faces a tougher test. Someone must prove the threat is serious, determine what intervention it warrants, and defend spending money on an event that might never happen. Failure has a funding mechanism. Prevention has a business case to make. Insurance can transfer part of a financial loss. It cannot restore missed production, repair damaged customer relationships, or undo the wider consequences of an industrial disruption. The challenge is making prevention as intelligible and investable as recovery. Knowing the risk isn't the same as managing it Industrial organizations rarely lack information. They receive risk-engineering reports, inspection findings, maintenance records and alerts from connected equipment. Yet information doesn't guarantee action. A temperature change, unusual vibration, or a deteriorating component has little meaning in isolation. Its significance depends on the asset's role in the operation. Is there redundancy? What production depends on it? What would a shutdown cost? Could a failure disrupt customers, supply chains or other facilities? These questions turn technical observations into business consequences. Without that translation, recommendations can remain in reports while maintenance teams address more immediate demands and capital committees fund projects with clearer returns. Industry has invested heavily in detecting changing conditions and predicting potential failures. Those capabilities matter. Still, knowing what might fail doesn't tell an organization which emerging risks deserve attention first. A relatively minor condition on a critical asset may represent far greater exposure than a severe condition on equipment with sufficient redundancy. The challenge is understanding what matters most, what the consequences could be, and where intervention will create the greatest value. Prevention needs to compete for capital Consider a manufacturer that identifies deterioration in a critical component on its main production line. Although the component hasn't failed, its condition is changing. The organization must compare the cost of replacing it during a planned shutdown with the lost output, repair time, and disruption that could follow an unplanned failure. The consequences, however, may extend well beyond that production line. A shutdown could affect customer deliveries, contractual commitments, supply-chain continuity and financial performance. What appears to be a maintenance decision may represent a much larger business risk. The appropriate response might be immediate repair, closer monitoring, a change in operating parameters or acceptance of the exposure. Someone must have the authority to make that decision and commit the necessary resources before the opportunity to intervene passes. Now multiply that challenge across hundreds of assets and facilities, each presenting different levels of exposure. The question is no longer simply whether an individual intervention is justified. It's which interventions deserve priority when resources are limited, and the consequences extend across the enterprise. For decades, industry has developed sophisticated ways to measure losses after they occur. We need comparable discipline in understanding the economic value of preventing those losses before they happen. Capital should not only be deployed to absorb loss. It should be possible to direct it intelligently toward preventing loss. The standard for resilience must rise Risk assessments, inspections and engineering recommendations are essential. Completing those processes, however, doesn't necessarily mean an organization has addressed its most consequential exposures. An inspection can establish that a process was followed. A risk assessment can document a vulnerability. Neither, by itself, demonstrates that the organization is becoming more resilient. Industrial risk isn't static. Asset conditions change, operational dependencies evolve, and an exposure that appeared manageable during a periodic assessment may become significantly more consequential. A recommendation without a named decision-maker and deadline is information, not control. Someone must have the authority to accept the exposure, fund the response or explain why another course is justified. Following the process is important, although it's not the same as preventing the loss. Insurance can help change the economics of prevention Insurers can make recommendations easier to act on by explaining the severity and urgency of an exposure, not simply recording that it exists. Brokers can connect risk-engineering findings with an organization's insurance and resilience priorities. Operators must determine whether to intervene or accept the exposure and take responsibility for the outcome. There is also a bigger opportunity here. Insurers and brokers possess extraordinary expertise in understanding, quantifying, and pricing risk. Much of that expertise has historically helped organizations prepare financially for potential losses. What if more of it could be applied to making prevention economically compelling before those losses occur? Imagine insurers, brokers, and industrial operators working from a more continuous, consequence-based understanding of emerging physical risk. Rather than relying primarily on historical losses and periodic assessments, they could better understand where exposure is developing, which conditions present the greatest business consequences, and where intervention could materially reduce risk. This wouldn't eliminate uncertainty or diminish the need for insurance. It could, however, create a stronger economic foundation for prevention and a more productive relationship between risk financing and operational decision-making. For decades, the insurance industry has helped businesses understand the financial consequences of what can go wrong. That expertise will remain indispensable, but the next opportunity is to help make the economics of what doesn't have to go wrong equally visible. We've become extraordinarily good at financing industrial failure. It's time to become just as disciplined about investing in its prevention. Andy Pruett

It's which interventions deserve priority when resources are limited, and the consequences extend across the enterprise. For decades, industry has developed sophisticated ways to measure losses after they occur. We need comparable discipline in understanding the economic value of preventing those losses before they happen. Capital should not only be deployed to absorb loss. It should be possible to direct it intelligently toward preventing loss. The standard for resilience must rise Risk assessments, inspections and engineering recommendations are essential. Completing those processes, however, doesn't necessarily mean an organization has addressed its most consequential exposures. An inspection can establish that a process was followed. A risk assessment can document a vulnerability. Neither, by itself, demonstrates that the organization is becoming more resilient. Industrial risk isn't static. Asset conditions change, operational dependencies evolve, and an exposure that appeared manageable during a periodic assessment may become significantly more consequential. A recommendation without a named decision-maker and deadline is information, not control. Someone must have the authority to accept the exposure, fund the response or explain why another course is justified. Following the process is important, although it's not the same as preventing the loss. Insurance can help change the economics of prevention Insurers can make recommendations easier to act on by explaining the severity and urgency of an exposure, not simply recording that it exists. Brokers can connect risk-engineering findings with an organization's insurance and resilience priorities. Operators must determine whether to intervene or accept the exposure and take responsibility for the outcome. There is also a bigger opportunity here. Insurers and brokers possess extraordinary expertise in understanding, quantifying, and pricing risk. Much of that expertise has historically helped organizations prepare financially for potential losses. What if more of it could be applied to making prevention economically compelling before those losses occur? Imagine insurers, brokers, and industrial operators working from a more continuous, consequence-based understanding of emerging physical risk. Rather than relying primarily on historical losses and periodic assessments, they could better understand where exposure is developing, which conditions present the greatest business consequences, and where intervention could materially reduce risk. This wouldn't eliminate uncertainty or diminish the need for insurance. It could, however, create a stronger economic foundation for prevention and a more productive relationship between risk financing and operational decision-making. For decades, the insurance industry has helped businesses understand the financial consequences of what can go wrong. That expertise will remain indispensable, but the next opportunity is to help make the economics of what doesn't have to go wrong equally visible. We've become extraordinarily good at financing industrial failure. It's time to become just as disciplined about investing in its prevention. A proposal to prevent an asset failure faces a tougher test. Someone must prove the threat is serious, determine what intervention it warrants, and defend spending money on an event that might never happen. Failure has a funding mechanism. items.title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.original_title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.rss_title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.rss_description: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop' PaulCarroll Tue, 11/10/2026 - 12:55 The notion that there must always be a "human in the loop" has become de rigueur in any discussion of AI implementation in business. The cynical side of me suspects that part of the reason is to reassure everyone that AI won't lead to mass layoffs, but there are also plenty of practical reasons to have humans check the work of AIs. Or maybe not. At least not for long. A recent article in Harvard Business Review argues that human supervisors quickly become numb and simply approve the recommendations of the AI as it becomes increasingly accurate. And I think the author has a point, based on what I've seen of human/AI interactions in semi-autonomous cars. There needs to be a better way. Let's have a look. Early in the development of its driverless cars, Google gave demo models to employees. Google warned them that the AI wasn't perfect and instructed them to have their hands on the wheel, always ready to take control. That worked... for a little while. A very little while. As the AI proved to be reliable, the drivers began to relax their hold on the wheel, then started to take their eyes off the road, then began reading or looking at their phones. When the car signaled that the drivers had to take over, they needed perhaps 10 seconds to fully reengage. Given that a car going 60mph travels nearly 300 yards in 10 seconds, Google realized its hybrid approach wouldn't work and committed to producing only cars that could be fully autonomous. Other makers of autonomous vehicles, most notably Tesla, continue to offer cars that take a hybrid, human/AI approach, but I think that's irresponsible (as I wrote at length a year ago). Now, an article in Harvard Business Review offers a similar view about the dangers of having a "human in the loop" to supervise work done by AIs. The author, a senior fellow at Cal, writes: "Decades of research on automation show that better automation systems lead to worse human safety layers; as automation grows more reliable, the people monitoring it grow complacent, their skills atrophy, and they become less attentive.... AI compounds the problem. Its failures sound as confident, fluent, and well-structured as its successes.... "Even when validation works and people catch errors, every correction is captured as training data. Each exception a person handles teaches the system to handle that exception; the better the data, the smaller the scope of human validation needed in the future." The article says the lack of reliability of the humans in the loop is actually just the start of the problem. He writes: "The larger problem with the human-in-the-loop organization, though, is that the entire blueprint reads the transformation backwards. It organizes the company around the shrinking frontier of what machines can’t yet do. But there’s a larger opportunity here. Because AI removes constraints, it enables new combinations of work, new decision rights, and new forms of value. Organizations, accordingly, have an opportunity to reorganize and 'rebundle' around those new decisions rather than the shrinking residue of the old work." He goes on to lay out how to think about rebundling: "Instead of asking which tasks the machine can take over, leading organizations should ask which new roles the technology makes possible, and then redesign the organization around them." He lists several steps that can lead you to new approaches, which seem intriguing and which you may want to explore. For now, though, I just want to make the point that "human in the loop" isn't a panacea, certainly not in the long term. The reviewers of AI work can quickly become as reliant on the AI as those Google employees who found themselves with their hands off the wheel, their eyes off the road and their minds far away from driving when a problem popped up in front of them. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll An HBR article argues that human supervisors quickly become unreliable as the AI becomes increasingly accurate. items.extracted_text: Cortina offers tangible benefits for bringing third-party capital into reinsurance: Aon's Nicholson - Artemis.bm Cortina offers tangible benefits for bringing third-party capital into reinsurance: Aon's Nicholson - Artemis.bm Cortina offers tangible benefits for bringing third-party capital into reinsurance: Aon’s Nicholson 16th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Aon and Blackstone’s newly launched Lloyd’s Cortina syndicate 1956 is expected to deliver tangible and important benefits towards helping bring third-party capital into the reinsurance market through Lloyd’s, Dave Nicholson, Global Client Leader, Aon Reinsurance Solutions told us in a recent interview. The heavily discussed reinsurance Cortina syndicate 1956 was recently launched by broker Aon and funds associated with asset manager, Blackstone. We also learned around the time of its launch that the London Bridge 2 insurance-linked securities structure was used towards funding the new syndicate. Cortina syndicate 1956 is set to begin underwriting from January 1st, 2027. Adopting a conventional lead/follow approach, the syndicate will provide dedicated, multi-year reinsurance capacity from institutional capital, bringing $500 million of capital to underwrite around $1.6 billion in premium. Speaking with Artemis, Nicholson explained how the syndicate’s structure adds discipline and governance, all of which will help towards bringing more third-party capital into the market. “One, you have that managing agent role as part of the Lloyd’s ecosystem, so you have underwriting expertise. With other vehicles, you’re setting up the box, and that’s it. With Cortina, there’s an extra party involved, which provides discipline, and then an additional party in the Lloyd’s marketplace, and that governance gives us a lot of comfort that it’s not Aon or candidly any other broker just promising this is going to be great results. There’s a lot of external parties that are helping to stress and challenge and underwrite the opportunity. These things have to be sustainable,” Nicholson told Artemis. Nicholson also emphasised that Lloyd’s has a great history of innovating, particularly through its insurance-linked securities structure London Bridge 2 PCC. Moreover, large asset managers have increasingly shown they prefer more flexible mechanisms to access reinsurance linked returns, instead of starting up new equity backed companies. Given this, we asked Nicholson to explain why Aon thinks a large asset management firm like Blackstone finds accessing Lloyd’s returns appealing. “Blackstone has established a number of innovative partnerships including various Lloyd’s Syndicates. Other asset managers certainly are interested, and many play in this space in different ways, whether that is an allocation to an ILS manager, a cat bond fund, etc. But I think the base case still remains, and it’s very similar to a theme that we’ve talked about as an industry, which is the diversified returns that come from, in particular, property cat. “But now, more broadly, as you look across the insurance industry, I think there is a huge element of that diversified exposure that forms an important part of portfolios. And these are new vehicles to bring that into a larger asset management structure,” Nicholson explained. Beyond Blackstone’s involvement, Cortina’s launch also raises a broader question for the reinsurance sector, whether other major asset managers will replicate this blueprint to deploy capital into Lloyd’s. According to Nicholson, wider adoption comes down to addressing clear capacity gaps, particularly in fast-growing, underinsured sectors like digital infrastructure. “We might see more vehicles like Cortina, and we should if they are good for clients. There has to be a demonstrable need and value, and we talked about the element of underinsured risk. I think that it is important that the industry as a whole continue to evolve and adapt, and proactively go after that risk. We spend a lot of time at Aon on the topic of digital infrastructure and data centers, where billions of dollars of additional insurance/reinsurance capacity are going to be needed. There’s huge investment in infrastructure, where private markets can provide an important signal of the risk around those types of things. To me, that’s going to be the real test: how do we continue to attack those problems and bring solutions for clients?,” Nicholson said. Further, Nicholson pointed out that scaling these third-party capital vehicles sustainably also relies on the guardrails established by the market itself, noting the importance of Lloyd’s recently introducing its framework for broker-led facilities. “One other important element to highlight is the Lloyd’s framework which they released around these facilities, which is another tangible point around that important role they play. And thinking about profitability of vehicles, protecting the broader marketplace, including many of those traditional partners, both insurers and reinsurers, and we put a lot of value in that and have a huge respect for what they’ve done,” Nicholson added. items.title: Two Architects of Key State AI Laws Come to Washington to Do It Again
items.original_title: Two Architects of Key State AI Laws Come to Washington to Do It Again
items.rss_title: Two Architects of Key State AI Laws Come to Washington to Do It Again
items.rss_description: Colorado’s Manny Rutinel and California’s Scott Wiener took on the artificial intelligence industry in their respective state capitals and won. Now they’ve arrived in Washington looking to do the same again. The two Democratic congressmen-elect, who as legislators back home …
items.extracted_text: Two Architects of Key State AI Laws Come to Washington to Do It Again Article 0 Comments Colorado’s Manny Rutinel and California’s Scott Wiener took on the artificial intelligence industry in their respective state capitals and won. Now they’ve arrived in Washington looking to do the same again. The two Democratic congressmen-elect, who as legislators back home were architects of the country’s first major state-level AI laws, are preparing to work hand-in-hand this time, in their drive for a federal law. Though they had never met in person before this week’s orientation for new lawmakers, Wiener and Rutinel have been phone friends for years, helping to advise one another through lobbying battles with the tech industry and tough committee votes. “We both took on this issue before it was considered popular, when it was more of a brutal fight with industry,” said Wiener, who spent the better part of the last three years laser-focused on passing AI safety laws as a California state senator representing San Francisco. The issue is popular now. From Ohio to Georgia to Florida, Democrats ran and won on demands for stronger regulation of AI and data centers, galvanizing voters amid increasingly widespread unease about the technology and concern about how AI will reshape society. Manny Rutinel, left, and Scott Wiener. Photographer: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images David Paul Morris/Bloomberg Rutinel and Wiener, both of whom won tight congressional races last week, are angling for spots on a potential AI select committee, which Democratic party leaders in the House are considering setting up to expedite action on federal AI regulation next year. “It is potentially one of the most defining issues of our time,” Rutinel said. “Right now we’ve got the largest corporations on the planet putting profits ahead of people and pushing reckless experiments that are putting our families’ health at risk, our kids’ futures at risk, our paychecks at risk.” The struggle ahead is likely to be fierce. Democratic leaders’ plans to push for significant AI guardrails next year confront a potential veto by President Donald Trump, who has steadfastly opposed stricter AI regulation and argued limitations on U.S. companies risk losing ground to China on a strategically pivotal technology. Financial markets are also heavily betting on rosy expectations for the industry’s future profitability, a vulnerability made clear once again by the hundreds of billions of dollars investors lost following disclosure of Nvidia Corp. co-founder Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Wiener and Rutinel come at the issue from different vantage points. Wiener, 56, serious and studious, is characteristic of the San Francisco community he represents: philosophical, bespectacled and deeply enmeshed in the complicated world of Bay Area tech workers. He came to the issue through salons examining AI safety. Rutinel, 31, a former climate lawyer who emphasizes his Colorado working-class roots, is atypical in the mostly coastal elite AI safety community. He started reading books on AI in 2018, then his interest grew more urgent as the technology developed. Both men are described by people close to them as tenacious legislators focused on details and concerned with the most dramatic risks AI could pose, including so-called “loss of control” — the concern that AI could eventually stop needing human intervention to continue improving. “We’re both dogged in wanting to get this done so that AI benefits humanity and doesn’t harm humanity,” Wiener said. Both their campaigns for Congress were backed by thousands of dollars in donations from AI safety advocates, including many at the biggest frontier AI labs, as well as millions from super political action committees focused on promoting candidates who want to regulate AI. Wiener’s signature legislation, vetoed in September 2024 and then signed into law in a stripped-down form a year later, addressed catastrophic risks, such as chemical, biological, radiological, or major cyber threats. Rutinel’s legislation, signed into law in 2024 and revised in May 2026, targeted AI-powered discrimination in employment, housing, finance, and healthcare. Wiener was known for his relentlessness in the California legislature, meeting one-on-one with every single lawmaker who voted on his bills, according to his former colleague California Assemblywoman Rebecca Bauer-Kahan. “He negotiates the language personally,” Bauer-Kahan said. “He met with every single one of our colleagues to walk them through his AI bill, to earn their support.” Rutinel, who was raised by a Latina immigrant single mother, worked at a McDonald’s for two years in high school and, by his account, sold his blood plasma more than 100 times to pay bills. He went on to earn a Yale law degree, working as a climate lawyer and activist before entering politics. Several people who have worked with Rutinel described him as charming and easy-going. “He’s very down to earth,” said Scott Wisor, policy director at AI safety organization Secure AI Project. “He’s familiar with the issues that day-to-day folks are going to be concerned about. He has a vision about where things are headed.” Former Democratic Oklahoma Representative Brad Carson, whose super PAC Public First spent $3.5 million boosting Wiener and $2.6 million for Rutinel, said he supported them because they were among the candidates “most involved in AI politics before they decided to run for Congress.” Wiener in particular, Carson said, persevered on the issue despite facing major backlash over his initial efforts to pass AI legislation in California. Under intense industry pressure, California Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed Wiener’s sweeping AI law, which Wiener ultimately pared down into the law passed in 2025. Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at AI safety group Encode, said Wiener was the first to take an “ambitious swing at directly regulating frontier AI risks,” including provisions in his initial legislation that would have made AI companies liable for catastrophic risks, required third parties to audit new AI models, and created a “kill switch,” or a mechanism to shut down AI products in an emergency. “These ideas were considered fringe at the time, and resulted in the legislation being vetoed,” Calvin said. “But now those sorts of ideas are at the center of the national policy discussion.” The more limited version Newsom ultimately signed requires AI developers to publicly disclose safety and security protocols and report critical incidents. Rutinel, meanwhile, is “both deeply knowledgeable and deeply sensitive to how AI could go good or bad and is deeply committed to being a national leader in it,” Carson said. That level of dedication makes a big difference in Congress, said Carson, a Capitol Hill veteran. “You have to have people who are going to be leaders in the caucus and make it a priority,” he said. “They’re both going to do so.” Copyright 2026 Bloomberg. items.rss_title: El Niño, Climate Change Supercharged Indonesia Fires, Study Says
items.rss_description: A strong El Niño and human-induced climate change fueled the hot and dry weather over Indonesia this year that sparked the country’s worst wildfire season in a decade, according to new research. El Niño was the driver of the severe …
items.extracted_text: El Niño, Climate Change Supercharged Indonesia Fires, Study Says Article 0 Comments A strong El Niño and human-induced climate change fueled the hot and dry weather over Indonesia this year that sparked the country’s worst wildfire season in a decade, according to new research. El Niño was the driver of the severe lack of rainfall, while climate change was the cause of high temperatures, a report by World Weather Attribution shows. Human-induced warming made hot and dry conditions about three times more likely, as well as more intense, researchers said. Indonesia’s worst fire season in years cloaked local towns and neighboring countries such as Singapore and Malaysia in toxic smog, prompting schools to close, straining diplomatic ties and crimping palm oil output. Poor rainfall from June through the end of October left the landscape bone-dry, making blazes often linked to slash-and-burn agricultural practices harder to contain. Related: SF Fed: El Niño Poses ‘Meaningful Risk’ of Higher Inflation in 2027 “El Niño turned off the taps, but fossil fuel emissions turned up the heat,” said Friederike Otto, a professor of climate science at Imperial College London and a co-author of the study published Friday. “Without rapidly transitioning away from fossil fuels and strengthened land-management protections, we will see more and much worse fire seasons like this in the future.” Climate change amplified the hotter conditions from August to October, making the seasonal heat about 1.6C hotter and more likely to occur, according to the study. Parts of Indonesia have also seen decades of deforestation and peatland draining, significantly increasing the fire risk, the authors wrote. The ongoing El Niño is estimated to have reduced Indonesia’s seasonal rainfall by about 50% this year, and together with higher temperatures, the country experienced “record breaking fire weather,” the report said. “Our analysis shows that climate change acts as a force multiplier during El Niño years,” said Theodore Keeping, an extreme weather and wildfire researcher at Imperial College London and lead author of the study. “When a strong El Niño hits, global warming makes the resulting fire weather significantly hotter, drier, and harder to contain.” Top photo: Soldiers and firefighters work to contain a wildfire in Banjarbaru, South Kalimantan on Oct. 13. items.extracted_text: Avec 11,5 milliards d’euros de cotisations en août 2026, l’assurance vie demeure un levier essentiel pour financer l’économie française et européenne - France Assureurs À 11,5 milliards d’euros, les cotisations en assurance vie sont en baisse de −6 % en août 2026 par rapport au même mois de 2025. Les prestations du mois d’août 2026 s’élèvent à 9,5 milliards d’euros, en hausse de +15 % par rapport à août 2025. Elles atteignent ainsi leur plus haut niveau depuis trois ans pour un mois d’août. La collecte nette s’établit à +2,0 milliards d’euros, en baisse de −1,9 milliard d’euros par rapport à celle d’août 2025. Depuis le début de l’année, elle s’élève à +43,5 milliards d’euros, supérieure de +6,9 milliards d’euros à celle de 2025 sur la même période. En août 2026, les cotisations en assurance vie s’élèvent à 11,5 milliards d’euros, en diminution de −6 % par rapport au même mois de 2025 où les cotisations avaient atteint un niveau exceptionnellement élevé (12,2 milliards d’euros, soit +27 % par rapport à août 2024). Les cotisations progressent de +3 % pour les supports en unités de compte (UC) mais diminuent pour les supports en euros (−10 %). Depuis début 2026, les cotisations atteignent 138,7 milliards d’euros, en hausse de +9,2 milliards d’euros, soit +7 % par rapport aux huit premiers mois de 2025. Cette dynamique positive concerne principalement les supports en UC (+10 %) et dans une moindre mesure ceux en euros (+5 %). La part des UC dans les cotisations s’établit à 37 % sur le mois d’août 2026 et se maintient à 40 % sur les huit premiers mois de l’année. À 9,5 milliards d’euros, les prestations du mois d’août 2026 sont en hausse de +15 % par rapport à août 2025. Cette augmentation est portée essentiellement par les supports en UC (+27 %), tandis que ceux en euros enregistrent une hausse de +11 %. Les prestations atteignent ainsi leur plus haut niveau pour un mois d’août depuis trois ans, avec notamment 2,4 milliards d’euros de prestations sur les supports en UC. Depuis le début de l’année, les prestations s’élèvent à 95,2 milliards d’euros, en légère progression de +2,3 milliards d’euros, soit +2 % par rapport aux huit premiers mois de 2025. Cette dynamique concerne principalement les supports en UC qui augmentent de +1,5 milliard d’euros, tandis que les prestations des supports en euros sont en hausse de +0,8 milliard d’euros. La collecte nette s’établit donc à +2,0 milliards d’euros en août 2026. Les supports en UC représentent l’essentiel de cette dynamique, avec une collecte nette positive de +1,9 milliard d’euros, tandis que les supports en euros enregistrent une collecte positive de +0,2 milliard d’euros. Depuis le début de l’année, la collecte nette s’élève à +43,5 milliards d’euros, supérieure de +6,9 milliards d’euros à celle de 2025 sur la même période. Les supports en UC concentrent une partie très majoritaire de cette collecte nette (+33,9 milliards d’euros), tandis que ceux en euros y contribuent à hauteur de +9,7 milliards d’euros. L’encours des contrats d’assurance vie atteint 2 171 milliards d’euros à fin août 2026, en hausse de +5,7 % sur un an (+117 milliards d’euros). Selon Paul ESMEIN, directeur général de France Assureurs : «En août 2026, les cotisations en assurance vie demeurent à un niveau élevé, à 11,5 milliards d’euros. Depuis le début de l’année, la dynamique de l’assurance vie confirme la confiance des Français dans ce produit d’épargne de long terme, qui leur permet de préparer leur avenir, tout en contribuant au financement de l’économie française. Avec 80 % de ses encours investis au sein de l’Union européenne et plus de la moitié sur le territoire français, l’assurance vie constitue un levier essentiel au service de la souveraineté nationale et européenne. » Pour en savoir plus sur l’assurance vie, cliquez ici. NB : l’arrondi d’un total ou d’une différence n’est pas nécessairement égal à la somme ou à la différence des arrondis de ses composantes. C’est parfois le cas entre la collecte nette d’une part et la différence entre les cotisations et les prestations d’autre part, lorsque ces grandeurs sont toutes trois arrondies en milliards d’euros. items.extracted_text: Microsoft 365 outage losses expected well-below cyber cat bond attachments: Euler ILS - Artemis.bm Microsoft 365 outage losses expected well-below cyber cat bond attachments: Euler ILS - Artemis.bm Microsoft 365 outage losses expected well-below cyber cat bond attachments: Euler ILS 16th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Estimated cyber insurance industry losses from the recent Microsoft 365 outage are projected to range between $100 million and $1 billion, a figure that will sit well-below the attachment points of any cyber catastrophe bonds currently in the market, according to Swiss insurance-linked securities investment manager Euler ILS Partners. While $100 million – $1 billion is a significant range, Euler ILS Partners importantly noted that market participants expect the final tally to land toward the lower end of that range. Crucially, the ILS investment manager pointed out that trigger levels across current cyber cat bond exposures sit significantly above these levels, meaning an industry loss of this scale is not expected to trouble any of the cyber catastrophe bonds currently in the market . At the same time, cyber risk analytics provider CyberCube has released its initial loss estimate from the event, stating that cyber insured losses will most likely come in below $100 million, with a conservative upper bound of $350 million. The outage, which is being referred to by CyberCube as “M364” began on November 12th when a failure in Microsoft Exchange Online, the email platform behind Outlook, reportedly cut off users across more than 70 countries. Key features in Teams, SharePoint, Copilot as well as Microsoft’s security tooling that depend on Exchange Online were all degraded, although their functions largely managed to continue working during the event. Severe disruption lasted for approximately 18 hours, and the entire event ran roughly 38 hours in total, which CyberCube explained is well beyond the eight-to-12 hour waiting periods common in contingent system failure cover. Microsoft has attributed the incident towards a technical issue that was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade, which surfaced following a more recent network change. There is no indication that the outage is the result of malicious or cyber activity. In addition, CyberCube also explained that M364 is expected to add 0% to 2% of global cyber premium to insurers’ loss ratios. That estimate is consistent with the Level 2 (moderate) tier the firm assigned in a client note on November 13th. Now, a few days following the event, CyberCube said it sees most outcomes clustering toward the lower end of its projected loss range, with the high estimate allowing headroom for information that could still emerge. Moreover, CyberCube also expects several factors to suppress insured losses, including that cover only responds where policies extend business interruption to non-malicious system failure at an outside provider, and that reported impacts focus on any inconvenience and productivity loss caused from the event, with workarounds widely available and little to no mention of lost revenue. The firm also said that email is not in the “critical transaction path of most businesses.” Jon Laux, CyberCube’s VP of Products and Analytics, commented: “This event once again reminds us how the technology world is concentrated in the hands of a few key providers. But it also reminds us that not all layers of the technology stack are equally critical to business operations. “Factors that informed our loss estimates include the relatively short duration of this event, the absence of any reported data corruption or leakage, and the ease with which companies fell back on alternative communication channels to email. items.extracted_text: VKB secures upsized €200m King Max Re cat bond renewal priced below guidance - Artemis.bm VKB secures upsized €200m King Max Re cat bond renewal priced below guidance - Artemis.bm VKB secures upsized €200m King Max Re cat bond renewal priced below guidance 16th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans VKB, the German domestic market insurance group, has successfully finalised its latest catastrophe bond sponsorship, securing the upsized target of €200 million of German multi-peril reinsurance protection from the King Max Re II DAC (Series 2026-1) issuance, while the notes have now been priced below the initial guidance, this publication understands. Versicherungskammer Bayern Versicherungsanstalt des oeffentlichen Rechts’ (VKB) ventured back to the catastrophe bond market in October to sponsor its second issuance, with this Series 2026-1 a renewal of sorts for the company’s soon to mature debut cat bond, the €175 million King Max Re 2023 , which matures in early January 2027. At first, VKB was targeting €175 million of German multi-peril reinsurance with this King Max Re II Series 2026-1 deal, which would fully replace the expiring cat bond protection, albeit attaching lower down than the soon to mature coverage. In our first update on this transaction, we learned that VKB was aiming to secure its latest catastrophe bond deal at reduced pricing as the spread guidance for the notes on offer for this issuance was reduced. Then, we were told that VKB was aiming to secure more German multi-peril reinsurance protection from investors, with the target for the King Max Re 2026-1 issuance raised to €200 million, while the pricing guidance was adjusted to the middle of the revised range . We’re now told that the targeted upsizing has been secured, as investor demand helped VKB secure more reinsurance than initially sought, while the pricing was finalised at a level below the initial guidance range indicating strong execution for the cat bond sponsor. As a result, King Max Re II DAC will now issue and sell a single €200 million tranche of King Max Re II Series 2026-1 Class A notes to cat bond investors. The notes will provide ceding reinsurer VKB Re, an internal reinsurer and risk pool for the group, with indemnity and per-occurrence triggered reinsurance protection against losses from a range of perils, including earthquake, hailstorm, flood and windstorm in Germany, running across a three year term beginning January 1st 2027. The €200 million of King Max Re II Series 2026-1 Class A cat bond notes come with an initial expected loss of 1.68%. Initially, these notes were first offered to cat bond investors with price guidance for a spread of between 3% and 3.25%, which was later revised to a lower spread of between 2.5% and 3% and then updated again to a 2.75% spread, so at the middle of that revised range. Which is where we’re now told the notes have been priced, to pay investors an initial risk interest spread of 2.75%. As a reminder, the maturing King Max Re 2023 cat bond had launched with an initial expected loss of 0.81% and priced to pay investors a risk interest spread of 5%, so a multiple of almost 6.2 times EL This new offering has secured the replacement coverage attaching at a lower-level in VKB’s reinsurance arrangements and with a meaningfully lower multiple of expected loss (around 1.64 times EL), reflecting the softened pricing environment and attractive conditions in the catastrophe bond market for sponsors. (Series 2026-1) issuance, Artemis has learned. Texas Farm Bureau Insurance returned to the catastrophe bond market for the second time at the start of the month, with a new Fish Pond Re issuance that looks set to be a renewal of its soon to mature debut cat bond deal. Texas Farm Bureau Insurance is the insurance arm of Texas’s largest farm organisation, the Texas Farm Bureau, a non-profit focused on its members from the agricultural community. Its debut catastrophe bond, sponsored in late 2023, secured it $255 million of Texas named storm reinsurance protection from the Fish Pond Re 2024-1 issuance, with that protection due to mature at the end of this year. Initially for this renewal, the Texas Farm Bureau Insurance Companies returned to the catastrophe bond market for its second sponsorship seeking $250 million of named storm reinsurance, from this Series 2026-1 issuance of notes by Fish Pond Re . Now, we’re told by sources that the target size for this issuance has been lifted by 60% to now $400 million, while at the same time the price guidance has been lowered. This new Fish Pond Re Ltd. issuance features two tranches of Series 2026-1 catastrophe bond notes, designed to provide the insurer with named storm reinsurance protection covering the state of Texas, on an indemnity trigger and per-occurrence basis running through to the end of 2030. What was initially a $125 million tranche of Series 2026-1 Class A notes are now being offered at $250 million in size. The Class A notes have an initial expected loss of 0.26% and were first offered with price guidance is in a range from 2.25% to 2.75%, but that has now been lowered to between 2% and 2.25%, we are told. What was a riskier $125 million tranche of Series 2026-1 Class B notes are now $150 million in terms of their offering size. The Class B notes come with an initial expected loss of 0.88% and were initially offered with price guidance in a range from 3% to 3.5%, but again we’re told this has fallen to a revised range of 2.75% to 3%. As a result, the Texas Farm Bureau looks on track to secure an upsized renewal of its catastrophe bond backed reinsurance protection, priced at the low-end of initial guidance or below, indicating a positive result for the sponsor. items.extracted_text: Uber Says Drivers’ License Data Stolen in Data Breach Article 0 Comments Uber said an unauthorized party used compromised credentials at a service provider to access its data, according to a notice posted on the California attorney general’s website. The notice, dated November 10, said the provider told Uber on October 9 that the credentials had been compromised and used to access Uber’s account with the provider. Uber severed its data connections with the provider and opened an investigation. On October 13, the investigation determined the party had used the credentials to access Uber data, and that the recipients’ personal information was among the data accessed, the notice said. The notice did not name the provider or list the data involved. TechCrunch reported on Friday that the provider was Fireworks AI and that the data included drivers’ license information. Uber and Fireworks AI did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. The notice said the incident affected about 1,873 Rhode Island residents. It also carried instructions for residents of the District of Columbia, Maryland, North Carolina, New York and Pennsylvania. Uber said it is offering affected people free credit monitoring and fraud assistance through Cyberscout, a TransUnion company. Recipients have 90 days from the date of the letter to enroll. The company said it had not identified any misuse of the data to date. (Reporting by Akash Sriram in Bengaluru Editing by Tasim Zahid) Copyright 2026 Reuters. Click for restrictions . items.rss_title: US Airlines Race to Recover From Longest Shutdown in Decades

items.extracted_text: US Airlines Race to Recover From Longest Shutdown in Decades Article 0 Comments U.S. airlines were scrambling at the start of a fresh week to resurrect their networks after the longest nationwide shutdown in more than two decades upended travel. The Federal Aviation Administration predicted airlines would be back to normal after Friday’s tech outage and a weekend of recovery efforts to reposition planes and crews. The world’s busiest aviation market has a long way to go. While cancellations are easing, data showed more than 10,000 services were still delayed by late Sunday. American Airlines Group Inc. and SkyWest Inc. were the hardest hit carriers, while key hubs Dallas-Fort Worth and Chicago O’Hare were the worst affected airports, showing a full recovery will likely take days. On Meet the Press on Sunday, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said flights should be “back to normal” by Monday. “What happens when we have a ground stop like what happened on Friday is we have airplanes and air crews that are out of position,” he said. “It takes some time for the airlines to re-choreograph all of their crews and aircraft.” Travelers check in at the United Airlines kiosks at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in Los Angeles, California, US, on Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. U.S. air travel struggled to recover Saturday from the longest nationwide flight suspension since the September 2001 terrorist attacks, with thousands of cancellations following an outage that laid bare the fragility of Americas aviation infrastructure. Photographer: Kyle Grillot/Bloomberg Major airlines including Delta Air Lines Inc. and Alaska Air Group Inc. said they are anticipating a more normal service or vastly reduced cancellations Monday. In a statement early Monday morning, American Airlines said it’s preparing to operate a “largely normal” schedule. “With crews and aircraft in position and favorable weather expected across our system, we are set up for a good start to the week and don’t anticipate additional broad cancellations related to this incredibly disruptive industry-wide event,” the airline said. Duffy said the issue was traced to the replacement of outdated copper wire at a remote location near El Dorado, Arkansas, by L3Harris Technologies Inc., and that a router there started flooding the air-traffic control system with connection attempts. That router is now undergoing testing at an L3Harris facility, Duffy said, adding that it was still unclear whether the issue was caused by the contractor’s “incompetence” or by a faulty router. “Those routers were purchased in 2001,” Duffy said on ABC’s This Week. “They were obsolete in 2006, and we still use them in 2026 just to underscore how old the network is.” The FAA said it is also examining equipment at a site in Amarillo, Texas, that may have also contributed to the overloads. The outage, which began at 3:30 p.m. New York time on Friday, led to instability at 17 of the 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers and spread to several Terminal Radar Approach Controls, the agency said. The shutdown was lifted at 8:15 p.m. on Friday. More than 17,000 flights in total have been canceled. Duffy said the government has looked at the risks that come with upgrading the FAA’s systems and there was no specific suggestion that the work on Friday would lead to a breakdown. “It’s worked thousands of times when we made the switchover,” Duffy said on CBS’s Face the Nation. “This time it didn’t.” Duffy focused his criticism on L3Harris. “L3Harris decades ago got the contract to run and own the network that operates communication for the FAA,” he said on NBC’s Meet the Press. “They own the network, which is why I’m asking for billions of dollars from Congress to build a brand new architecture of a network by the best companies in the world, including AT&T, Verizon, and Lumen.” L3Harris said in a statement Saturday that it’s cooperating with the FAA in its investigation. The company said that, with its telco partners and the FAA, it has “completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system.” In the wake of the ground stop, Duffy said the Trump administration will send Congress an emergency funding request for $50 billion to modernize the FAA’s aging infrastructure, saying the money should have been approved much earlier. “I can’t blame Republicans or Democrats, because it’s all of them,” he said on Meet the Press. “This goes back 20, 25, 30 years of a lack of investment.” Scott Kirby, the CEO of United Airlines Holdings Inc., said that transportation has always been a bipartisan issue. “I’ve spoken to leaders on both sides of the aisle in the last 24 hours and can confirm that they’re committed to modernizing the U.S. ATC system while holding the FAA accountable at the same time,” he said in a statement. Travelers check in at the United Airlines kiosks at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in Los Angeles, California, U.S., on Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. U.S. air travel struggled to recover Saturday from the longest nationwide flight suspension since the September 2001 terrorist attacks, with thousands of cancellations following an outage that laid bare the fragility of Americas aviation infrastructure. Photographer: Kyle Grillot/Bloomberg President Donald Trump, who was silent on the FAA stoppage until Sunday morning, backed up the push for Congress to approve a massive infusion of cash. “Much of our current air control system is 50 years old — RIDICULOUS!” he said in a social media post. “We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve.” Last year, Congress provided the FAA with $12.5 billion to carry out the modernization effort, but Duffy has said more money is needed. He initially requested an additional $30 billion but upped that to $50 billion after Friday’s breakdown. House Democrats, meanwhile, said that 15 months after Congress approved the $12.5 billion for air-traffic control improvements, the Transportation Department has obligated $4.3 billion and only spent $1 billion. Duffy said on ABC that Congress put strict boundaries on that spending and he needs more flexible funding to carry out the telecom upgrades. items.rss_title: Uber Says US Drivers’ License Data Stolen in Data Breach

items.extracted_text: Uber Says US Drivers’ License Data Stolen in Data Breach Article 0 Comments Uber said an unauthorized party used compromised credentials at a service provider to access its data, according to a notice posted on the California attorney general’s website. The notice, dated November 10, said the provider told Uber on October 9 that the credentials had been compromised and used to access Uber’s account with the provider. Uber severed its data connections with the provider and opened an investigation. On October 13, the investigation determined the party had used the credentials to access Uber data, and that the recipients’ personal information was among the data accessed, the notice said. The notice did not name the provider or list the data involved. TechCrunch reported on Friday that the provider was Fireworks AI and that the data included drivers’ license information. Uber and Fireworks AI did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. The notice said the incident affected about 1,873 Rhode Island residents. It also carried instructions for residents of the District of Columbia, Maryland, North Carolina, New York and Pennsylvania. Uber said it is offering affected people free credit monitoring and fraud assistance through Cyberscout, a TransUnion company. Recipients have 90 days from the date of the letter to enroll. The company said it had not identified any misuse of the data to date. (Reporting by Sriram in Bengaluru Editing by Tasim Zahid) Copyright 2026 Reuters. Click for restrictions . Ceres, a US-based non-profit organisation that leads a national coalition of investors, environmental organisations and other public interest groups working to address global sustainability challenges, has welcomed a new General Counsel opinion letter from the California Department of Insurance clarifying how parametric insurance can be effectively deployed across the state’s admitted market. items.extracted_text: New California legal opinion sets guardrails for parametric insurance deployment: Ceres - Artemis.bm New California legal opinion sets guardrails for parametric insurance deployment: Ceres - Artemis.bm New California legal opinion sets guardrails for parametric insurance deployment: Ceres 16th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Ceres, a US-based non-profit organisation that leads a national coalition of investors, environmental organisations and other public interest groups working to address global sustainability challenges, has welcomed a new General Counsel opinion letter from the California Department of Insurance clarifying how parametric insurance can be effectively deployed across the state’s admitted market. Issued in response to a July request from Ceres, the opinion letter gives insurers, communities, and consumers a clear legal framework for a tool capable of delivering disaster payouts within days or weeks of a wildfire, flood, or extreme heat event. According to Ceres, the legal opinion is expected to clear a path for wider parametric adoption across California, helping to close protection gaps caused by increasingly frequent extreme weather. “Weather-related disasters are hitting California families, businesses, and local budgets harder every year, and too many of those costs fall outside traditional insurance,” commented Jaclyn de Medicci Bruneau, Ceres’ director of insurance. “This opinion gives insurers the clarity they need to bring parametric products to market and gives consumers the protections they deserve. California has done the groundwork and put strong guardrails in place. Now the opportunity is to put this tool to work for the communities that need it most.” In Ceres’ published 10-Point Plan for the Insurance Industry, parametric insurance and other emerging financial instruments are identified as key mechanisms and approaches for providing faster payouts and broader coverage options. Ceres noted that the approach is already protecting people and ecosystems globally. The firm highlighted how India uses a heat insurance program run by a trade group and nonprofit, which helps outdoor workers cover lost income when temperatures spike. While in Mexico and Hawaii, reef insurance policies held by The Nature Conservancy pay out after hurricanes strike, which allows local teams to quickly repair damaged coral. This happened most recently when Hurricane Lala triggered Hawaiʻi’s policy this year, Ceres said. “California has been laying out the groundwork since 2019. Commissioner Ricardo Lara’s Climate Insurance Working Group recommended parametric coverage in its 2021 report. The California Department of Insurance has since supported a community-based parametric flood insurance pilot in Isleton, a coastal resilience and insurance effort in Imperial Beach, extreme heat coverage for Los Angeles’ street vendors, and research into insuring urban forests,” Ceres added. “Since 2019, we have pushed for creative solutions to protect Californians from the growing costs of climate change. Parametric insurance can get money into people’s hands quickly after a disaster, when they need it most. This opinion makes clear that when these products are insurance, they will be held to California’s consumer protection standards, so people know what they are buying and rates are fair,” said California Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara. The opinion letter extends that work by addressing a threshold issue: when does a parametric product constitute insurance? Under the opinion, a product qualifies if it meets three requirements: the buyer has an insurable interest, the product genuinely transfers risk, and the buyer can show proof of loss. Ceres also noted that qualifying parametric products are subject to CDI oversight and the California Insurance Code, as well as Proposition 103 where applicable, including its prior rate-approval requirements. The opinion letter also outlines several best practices for consumer protection. On transparency and basis risk, the guidance calls for triggers to be based on objective, verifiable third-party data, and for payout terms to be written in language a reasonable purchaser can understand, and the use of high-quality modeling and periodic recalibration as climate risks evolve. The letter also stresses that parametric coverage should be marketed as a complement to, rather than as a sole replacement for traditional insurance, with clear disclosures put in place that state payouts may differ from actual losses. Finally, in order to ensure data integrity, dispute resolution, and regulatory oversight, insurers are expected to maintain documentation of trigger calculations and data sources, while providing policyholders with audit and appeal rights, and also apply traditional prudential standards, and submit complete rate filings for review before products are sold. The letter also highlights how parametric insurance offers many additional benefits that can help strengthen resilience. “First, due to the need for minimal loss/damage assessments and because the payout is a set amount , parametric insurance can provide faster payouts. Additionally, these products can provide increased flexibility, in that the payouts can be used for almost anything and are not tied to living expenses or temporary repairs as with a traditional indemnity policy,” the letter reads. “Lastly, these products can reduce the risk of fraud due to their reliance on objective triggers. Parametric products provide a payment amount that is generally predetermined, standardized, and based on an independently verified trigger, minimizing opportunities for manipulation of the claims process.” With this framework in place, Ceres said that the next Insurance Commissioner, who is set to take office in January 2027, will be responsible for reviewing parametric insurance rate filings and overseeing these products as they come to market. “Recovery is fastest when resources arrive before a crisis turns into a long-term setback. Parametric insurance, built on reliable data and independent, clear triggers, can help communities bridge the financial gap between a disaster and the longer process of rebuilding. California’s framework offers a model for how to pair financial innovation with accountability, integrating a new tool into the state’s comprehensive disaster recovery strategy,” said Newsha Ajami, founding director, Program on Governance for Risk, Resilience, and Recovery (GR3), Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability.
